title: How Lansing Hired the Team to Build Its Housing Pods
sourceTitle: How Lansing Hired the Team to Build Its Housing Pods
headline: Lansing Hired NOVA Housing Pods Without Bids
attribution: Rhinoceros Media — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Lansing is building a new project called NOVA. It will have 50 small houses for 66 people who do not have a home. The city hired three companies to build and run this project. However, the city did not use a normal bidding process for these companies.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The nonprofit group that will run the site was the only one to apply. The architect was hired without any bids. The construction company was hired after the city asked for bids twice but got no answers.

The city says these are legal ways to hire when no one else applies. One company gave $5,000 to the mayor’s political fund in December 2025. This was eight months before the city chose them for the project.

There is no proof that this was wrong, but people want to see the records. The city has not shared the contract details or the reasons for the architect hire. Residents want to know how the city spends $1.9 million of public money.

evidence: The three companies building and running Lansing's NOVA housing-pod project were each hired without a completed competitive bid.
NOVA would place 50 modular housing pods and a resource center on Ingham County land on South Cedar Street, for up to 66 people leaving homelessness.

NOVA is a public project spending more than $1.9 million on site work and construction to house people with nowhere to live, and residents are entitled to check how the city chose the firms spending that money.
A1-A2.headline: Lansing Hired NOVA Housing Pods Without Bids

pages.text: Lansing’s NOVA housing-pod project, designed to provide shelter for 66 people experiencing homelessness, has faced scrutiny regarding its procurement process. The city hired three separate firms to manage, design, and build the site, yet none of these contracts were awarded through a standard competitive bidding process.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The operator, Detroit Rescue Mission Ministries, was the sole applicant for the $952,000-a-year contract. The city’s consultant noted that other agencies lacked the capacity to participate. Meanwhile, the architect was hired via a “sole source” agreement, and the general contractor, Clark Construction, was selected after two failed attempts to solicit bids.

While these methods are legally permissible when the market fails to respond, they have left the public without a way to compare prices or approaches. Questions have also emerged regarding a $5,000 donation made by Clark Construction to the mayor’s political fund in December 2025.

Although officials maintain that each hire has a valid explanation and there is no evidence of wrongdoing, the lack of transparency remains a concern. Residents are currently unable to access the specific contract terms or the justification for the architect’s selection. As the city spends $1.9 million on this project, the public continues to seek clarity on how these vendors were chosen.

B1-B2.headline: Lansing Hired NOVA Housing Pods Without Bids

pages.text: The NOVA housing-pod initiative in Lansing, Michigan, intended to accommodate 66 individuals transitioning out of homelessness, has become the subject of public inquiry due to its unconventional procurement history. The project, which utilizes $1.9 million in public funds for site development and the installation of 50 modular units, has seen all three primary vendors—the operator, the architect, and the general contractor—secured without the benefit of a competitive bidding process.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The operator, Detroit Rescue Mission Ministries, secured a $952,000 annual contract as the solitary respondent to the city’s request for proposals. The city’s homelessness consultant, Kimberly Coleman, attributed this to a lack of capacity among larger agencies. The architect was retained through a “sole source” designation, a mechanism that bypasses competitive bidding entirely, though the city has provided no public justification for this specific choice.

Furthermore, Clark Construction was appointed as the general contractor following two unsuccessful solicitations. While the city asserts that these actions are lawful shortcuts necessitated by a non-responsive market, the absence of competitive benchmarks prevents residents from evaluating the fiscal efficiency of these agreements. Compounding these concerns is a $5,000 contribution made by Clark Construction to the mayor’s political fund in December 2025, roughly eight months prior to the announcement of their selection for the NOVA contract.

While officials emphasize that this donation predates the failed bidding rounds and does not constitute evidence of impropriety, the timing has invited skepticism. The city has yet to release the executed contracts, bid records, or the rationale for the sole-source architectural hire. Consequently, the public remains unable to verify the terms governing the expenditure of these significant funds, leaving residents to rely on official assurances regarding the integrity of the selection process.

title: Lansing City Council Meeting: August 24, 2026
headline: Lansing City Council Meeting: August 24, 2026
attribution: Rhinoceros Media — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: On August 24, many people went to the Lansing City Council meeting. They talked for hours. They told the council they do not want automated license plate reader cameras. They want the city to stop using them. The council voted 7 to 1 to ask the city and the police to end the contracts with Flock Safety.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: This vote is a request. It does not remove the cameras yet. The council members said they might write a new law to stop the cameras later. The meeting was long. The Committee of the Whole scheduled for that evening was canceled, so the regular session was the only meeting. Many people spoke in person.

The clerk noted about 30 written communications, all but one supporting the resolution, and dozens of residents spoke in person; by the presiding officer's count and a closing speaker's, the comments approached 100. The opposition was not quite unanimous. They were the exception in a room that ran heavily the other way.

The council also talked about a developer fee. As we reported then, the staff report did not state the one-time fee the developer would pay for that public property, and no figure was mentioned on the floor. On August 24 the council supplied it.

evidence: — For most of a four-hour meeting on August 24, residents told the Lansing City Council the same thing over and over: they don't want the city's automated license plate reader cameras, and they want the contracts behind them gone.
The vote does not, by itself, remove a single camera.
The resolution is a request: it puts the council on record and sends the matter to Mayor Andy Schor and Police Chief Robert Backus, who control the contracts.

pages.text: During a four-hour session on August 24, the Lansing City Council faced significant public pressure regarding automated license plate reader cameras. Residents, including teachers and community advocates, urged officials to terminate existing contracts with Flock Safety. The Committee of the Whole scheduled for that evening was canceled, so the regular session was the only meeting.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: Following hours of public testimony, the council voted 7 to 1 to request that the city and the police department end these agreements. Kost moved it without reading it, saying the public comment had made the case. While the vote signals a clear stance, it is not legally binding.

The resolution is a request: it puts the council on record and sends the matter to Mayor Andy Schor and Police Chief Robert Backus, who control the contracts. Spadafore voted no, saying he was not comfortable adopting a resolution broader than the evening's discussion on roughly four days' notice and preferred a collaborative ordinance.

The clerk noted about 30 written communications, all but one supporting the resolution, and dozens of residents spoke in person; by the presiding officer's count and a closing speaker's, the comments approached 100. The opposition was not quite unanimous. They were the exception in a room that ran heavily the other way. Regarding other business, the council addressed a developer fee.

As we reported then, the staff report did not state the one-time fee the developer would pay for that public property, and no figure was mentioned on the floor. On August 24 the council supplied it. What the council can do on its own, several members said, is write an ordinance with binding rules, and two of them said they intend to try. The resolution's limits drew the last word of the night.

That account, which this outlet has not independently verified, sits awkwardly against the chief's earlier description of logs kept and reviewed since 2024; the chief was no longer present to reconcile the two. The organizer also noted that the Michigan State Capitol Commission is moving to add six of its own Flock cameras and an autonomous drone around the Capitol complex, and he urged the council to pass a binding ordinance.

B1-B2.headline: Lansing City Council Meeting: August 24, 2026

pages.text: On August 24, the Lansing City Council convened for a four-hour meeting dominated by intense public opposition to the city's deployment of automated license plate reader cameras. Residents, representing a diverse cross-section of the community, consistently demanded the termination of contracts with Flock Safety. The Committee of the Whole scheduled for that evening was canceled, so the regular session was the only meeting. The public discourse was extensive.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Lansing, Michigan skyline 2024

pages.text: The clerk noted about 30 written communications, all but one supporting the resolution, and dozens of residents spoke in person; by the presiding officer's count and a closing speaker's, the comments approached 100. The opposition was not quite unanimous. They were the exception in a room that ran heavily the other way. Kost moved it without reading it, saying the public comment had made the case.

Ultimately, the council voted 7 to 1 to formally request that the administration and the police department cease these operations. Kost, Nevarez Martinez, Adam Hussain, Tamera Carter, Jeremy Garza, Clara Martinez, and Pehlivanoglu voted yes. Spadafore voted no, saying he was not comfortable adopting a resolution broader than the evening's discussion on roughly four days' notice and preferred a collaborative ordinance. The vote does not, by itself, remove a single camera.

The resolution is a request: it puts the council on record and sends the matter to Mayor Andy Schor and Police Chief Robert Backus, who control the contracts. What the council can do on its own, several members said, is write an ordinance with binding rules, and two of them said they intend to try. The resolution's limits drew the last word of the night.

That account, which this outlet has not independently verified, sits awkwardly against the chief's earlier description of logs kept and reviewed since 2024; the chief was no longer present to reconcile the two. The organizer also noted that the Michigan State Capitol Commission is moving to add six of its own Flock cameras and an autonomous drone around the Capitol complex, and he urged the council to pass a binding ordinance.

In separate business, the council finalized a developer fee that had remained unresolved. As we reported then, the staff report did not state the one-time fee the developer would pay for that public property, and no figure was mentioned on the floor. On August 24 the council supplied it. This action, alongside the debate over surveillance technology, underscored the council's ongoing efforts to balance development interests with public oversight.

The resolution is a request: it puts the council on record and sends the matter to Mayor Andy Schor and Police Chief Robert Backus, who control the contracts.
